paras: The attempted lynching of James Semmes, also reported as Jim Seams, followed the shooting of a Tuscaloosa County deputy sheriff near Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on January 24, 1888. Semmes, a Black man the deputy had come to arrest on a warrant, was accused of killing him and escaped, and he was captured and wounded by the sheriff's posse three days later. According to a Birmingham dispatch, an effort to lynch him was made at Tuscaloosa, and the sheriff moved him to Birmingham under guard.

A dispatch from Tuscaloosa dated January 24 said that Deputy Sheriff Antrey, who held a warrant for Semmes's arrest, went with an assistant to Semmes's house at Hall's Station that morning. By the officers' account, Semmes fired a gun through a crack in the door and hit Antrey in the neck and chest with buckshot, killing him instantly. He then ran out, knocked the other officer down, and escaped, while a posse from Tuscaloosa took up the chase.

The Atlanta Constitution's weekly news summary, which gave the names as Autry and "Jim Starnes" and the place as "Maxwell's station," called the fugitive "a noted desperado." The same summary said that "a large posse of white men" was searching the country for him and that "if he is caught he will be strung up."

On Friday, January 27, the posse caught him in the Big Sandy neighborhood, about twenty-five miles south of Tuscaloosa, after what the report called "a desperate battle." He was shot several times but not fatally, and the same report noted "considerable talk of lynching." A special dispatch from Birmingham dated January 28 said that an effort to lynch him had been made at Tuscaloosa and that the sheriff had brought him to Birmingham under a strong guard for safekeeping.

In Birmingham, the dispatch said, the prisoner "talked freely about the crime" and remarked that he expected to be hanged but that "it was all right, as he had killed his man." No later report of an indictment, trial, or execution was found in the coverage, and none names anyone who took part in the effort to lynch him.

The shooting reached readers through a Tuscaloosa special to the Montgomery Advertiser, which ran on January 25 in the New York Sun, the Savannah Morning News, the Palatka Daily News, and the Richmond Dispatch, and as a brief in the Indianapolis Journal. Its headlines put the race of the accused first, as in the Sun's "A Deputy Sheriff Killed by a Negro" and the Savannah paper's "His Murderer a Negro for Whom He Had a Warrant." Every version told the story from the officers' side, and none reported anything from Semmes himself until after his capture.

Later coverage was thin: one condensed telegram in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reported the capture and the lynching talk, and the Atlanta Constitution carried both the threat and the Birmingham special. The Constitution reported the threat to string him up without comment and headlined its Birmingham item with his own words, "He Had Killed His Man." News-brief columns such as the Hillsboro Recorder's and The Gale's ran a one-sentence brief on the deputy's death into February, without mentioning the lynching attempt.

The papers spelled the names in several ways: the accused appears as Semmes, Semms, Seams, and Starnes, and the deputy as Antrey, Antry, Autrey, and Autry, with the Hillsboro Recorder giving his initials as J. M. The first wire placed the shooting on the morning of January 24, while the Wheeling telegram said Tuesday night, and only the Constitution's weekly summary named the place as Maxwell's station rather than Hall's Station.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of James Semmes
bases: After a sheriff's posse captured and wounded the accused, an effort to lynch him was reported at Tuscaloosa, and the sheriff moved him to Birmingham to prevent it (A6, A8).

Semmes survived: he was wounded in the capture and then held by the sheriff in Birmingham after a reported effort to lynch him at Tuscaloosa (A6, A8). The attempt was illegal and was prompted by the killing of the deputy, but no report gives the size of the would-be lynchers (A8).

The killing and escape come from the Advertiser wire (A2, A3), while the capture, the talk of lynching and the attempt appear in separate later dispatches (A6, A8, A7); only A8 reports an actual attempt.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution weekly synopsis
accounts.gist: Deputy Autry was killed near Maxwell's station arresting Jim Starnes; a large posse of white men was searching, and he would be 'strung up' if caught.

framing.detail: The first-day wire ran under headlines naming the race of the accused, 'A Deputy Sheriff Killed by a Negro' and 'His Murderer a Negro for Whom He Had a Warrant', and gave only the officers' side.
The Atlanta Constitution reported the threat to string him up and the lynching effort matter-of-factly, headlining his remark 'He Had Killed His Man.'

conflicts.note: The deputy's name also varies: Antrey/Antry in the first wire, Autrey (A6), Autry (A7, A8), J. M. Autry (A10). These look like spelling variants of the same two men.
Both put it on Tuesday, January 24; the dated Tuscaloosa dispatch (A2) is closer to the event.
Only the Constitution's weekly synopsis gives Maxwell's station; the dated dispatches say Hall's Station.

record_check.dossier: January 24 is the date the deputy was shot; the capture was January 27 and the lynching effort was reported in a January 28 dispatch.
Pursuit and shooting by the posse, plus an effort to lynch at Tuscaloosa and removal to Birmingham under guard.
He was at large during the manhunt, but in the sheriff's custody when the lynching effort was made at Tuscaloosa.
The sheriff's posse, called 'a large posse of white men', did the shooting; the would-be lynchers are not named.
